units.title: Unit 57 — Social English
learningObjectives: Select natural informal expressions for sympathy, irritation, invitations, surprise and partings.
Avoid literal combinations when intensifying hope, pleasure, delight or anticipation.
Use nuanced social collocations with appropriate warmth, politeness and register.

items.example: We did not have much luck finding an affordable hotel near the station.
items.note: With negative expressions, have much luck means be unsuccessful in an attempt.

items.example: Maya had a bright idea for making the weekly meetings shorter.
items.note: Bright idea often means a clever suggestion; in some contexts it can be sarcastic.

items.example: The thought occurred to me that we could share the taxi home.
items.note: Occur to expresses a sudden idea entering someone’s mind; it is not happen to.

items.pt: ter trabalho ou se dar ao incômodo
items.example: Please do not go to any trouble preparing food just for me.
items.note: Go to trouble means take extra effort or inconvenience, especially in polite exchanges.

items.example: My neighbour had a go at me for leaving the gate unlocked.
items.note: Informal British usage meaning criticise someone angrily; distinct from have a go at a task, meaning try.

items.example: His constant criticism really got to her after a few weeks.
items.note: Informal get to someone means upset or irritate them emotionally, not physically reach them.

items.pt: ser duro ou exigente com alguém
items.example: Try not to be too hard on your brother; he has just started the job.
items.note: Being hard on someone means treating them with excessive criticism or severity.

items.example: I meant no harm when I asked about the change in your plans.
items.note: Mean no harm says no offence or injury was intended; intentions do not guarantee no harm occurred.

items.example: I cannot bear the thought of losing all those family photographs.
items.note: Often appears with can’t or couldn’t; bear the thought of is followed by a noun or -ing form.

items.pt: perder o sono por causa de algo
items.example: A minor typo is not something you should lose sleep over.
items.note: Commonly used in negative advice, often meaning worry excessively rather than literally miss sleep.

items.example: I had only accepted the job an hour ago, but news travels fast around this town.
items.note: A fixed informal comment when information spreads sooner than expected.

items.word: come as a bit of a shock
items.example: The sudden change of venue came as a bit of a shock to the organisers.
items.note: Come as a shock describes unexpected news, usually unsettling; a bit softens the impact.

items.example: To be brutally honest, I do not think this proposal is ready for approval.
items.note: Brutally honest signals an unusually direct opinion and can sound tactless.

items.example: After three days of heavy rain, the clear skies were a welcome relief.
items.note: Welcome relief is a positive change after something tiring or unpleasant.

items.example: I said, “I know the feeling,” when Rafael mentioned how tiring the move had been.
items.note: Informal empathetic response meaning that you have experienced something similar.

items.example: The presenter is sharp-tongued, but her criticism is often insightful.
items.note: Describes someone whose remarks are cutting or unkind; it is not a compliment about eloquence.

items.word: be glad to see the back of someone
items.pt: ficar feliz de se livrar de alguém
items.example: After months of arguments, they were glad to see the back of their difficult flatmate.
items.note: Informal, often impolite phrase meaning feel relieved when someone leaves.

items.pt: estar a fim de fazer algo
items.example: Would you be up for a short walk after dinner?
items.note: Informal be up for means willing or interested in doing something.

items.pt: fazer uma boa despedida para alguém
items.example: We organised a farewell dinner to give our retiring manager a good send-off.
items.note: Give a send-off means celebrate someone’s departure with a positive farewell.

items.example: I will be late, but I should still make it to the party by nine.
items.note: Make it to an event means manage to attend or arrive, despite obstacles.

items.example: The simple reason we changed the schedule was that the venue was unavailable.
items.note: Introduces a straightforward explanation, typically followed by is that or why.

items.example: I have been on the go since early morning and need a break.
items.note: Informal be on the go means be constantly busy or active.

items.example: After the overnight journey, all I wanted was a decent night’s sleep.
items.note: Decent means sufficiently restful or good-quality; a natural pairing with night’s sleep.

items.example: He could not face the thought of repeating the entire examination.
items.note: Often negative; face the thought of highlights unwillingness to contemplate something.

items.example: Saying the bus was one minute late sounded like a feeble excuse for missing the meeting.
items.note: Feeble describes an excuse as unconvincing or weak.

items.example: Give me a ring when your train arrives and I will meet you outside.
items.note: Informal, especially British English, for telephone someone; not deliver a physical ring.

items.pt: mandar um e-mail rápido a alguém
items.example: Drop me an email once you have checked the final figures.
items.note: Drop someone an email is an informal request to send a short message.

items.example: I hope the change in our booking did not cause you any trouble.
items.note: Cause trouble is idiomatic; bring someone trouble is not the normal polite formula.

items.example: We did not want to put our hosts to any trouble over breakfast.
items.note: Put someone to trouble stresses inconvenience imposed on them; often appears with any.

items.example: I am really looking forward to meeting the whole team next week.
items.note: Really, not very, naturally intensifies look forward to; to is a preposition followed by a noun or -ing.

items.example: We very much look forward to welcoming you to the conference.
items.note: Very much is a natural, slightly more formal intensifier with look forward to.

items.example: We sincerely hope that the repairs will be finished before winter.
items.note: Sincerely or very much can modify hope; strongly hope is not the usual pairing.

items.example: I was absolutely delighted when my sister announced her engagement.
items.note: Absolutely is a natural intensifier for the extreme adjective delighted; very delighted is generally avoided.

items.example: It was a great pleasure to work with such a supportive group.
items.note: Use great pleasure as a polite expression, not big pleasure.

items.example: After the long mountain hike, everyone was absolutely shattered.
items.note: Informal, especially British English, for extremely tired; a natural emphatic intensifier.

items.pt: ter uma boa noite de sono
items.example: I need to have a decent night’s sleep before tomorrow’s early flight.
items.note: The verb have naturally combines with a decent night’s sleep when expressing a need for rest.

units.title: Unit 58 — Discussing issues
learningObjectives: Discuss assurances, promises, accusations and commitments in formal contexts.
Frame and respond to questions with precise collocations for discussion and debate.
Differentiate agreement, polite disagreement, public denials and contractual obligations.

items.example: The airline gave repeated assurances that passengers would receive refunds.
items.note: Give assurances that introduces repeated promises or emphatic statements intended to reassure.

items.example: He broke a promise to call his grandparents every Sunday.
items.note: Break a promise means fail to do what one promised, contrasting with keep a promise.

items.example: The supplier offered an explanation for the unexpected delivery delay.
items.note: Offer an explanation is idiomatic for providing a reason; often followed by for.

items.example: Sharing her private messages would betray her trust.
items.note: Betray trust means violate confidence placed in someone, not simply disagree with them.

items.example: The director rejected the charge that safety warnings had been ignored.
items.note: Charge can mean an allegation; reject a charge states firm disagreement, not a legal dismissal.

items.example: Our council kept its promise to reopen the public library.
items.note: Keep a promise means fulfil it, in direct contrast to break or go back on a promise.

items.example: The company went back on its promise to protect the remaining jobs.
items.note: Go back on is a phrasal verb meaning fail to honour or reverse a commitment.

items.example: Each participant made a commitment to attend the weekly sessions.
items.note: Make a commitment can be followed by to plus an infinitive or a noun phrase.

items.example: The board reaffirmed its commitment to improving accessibility.
items.note: Reaffirm means explicitly state an existing commitment again, not make a new one.

items.example: Please give a straight answer instead of changing the subject.
items.note: Straight answer means a clear, direct and candid response.

items.example: The spokesperson dodged the question about who had authorised the payment.
items.note: Dodge a question means avoid answering it rather than simply misunderstand it.

items.example: The audience put a difficult question to the guest speaker.
items.note: Put a question to someone is somewhat formal and natural in interviews and discussions.

items.example: The organisation opened new channels of communication with local residents.
items.note: Channels of communication are the routes or mechanisms through which information is exchanged.

items.example: She took a moment to frame her question without sounding confrontational.
items.note: Frame a question means choose its wording or structure thoughtfully.

items.pt: responder a perguntas feitas ao vivo
items.example: The engineer fielded questions from reporters after the presentation.
items.note: Field questions means handle or respond to questions, especially from an audience.

items.example: The committee finally confronted the issue of unequal access to services.
items.note: Confront an issue means address it directly rather than avoid it.

items.example: That is a fair comment, although I still disagree with your proposed solution.
items.note: Fair comment acknowledges that a criticism or observation is reasonable.

items.example: The rescue team managed to establish communication with the stranded climbers.
items.note: Establish communication means create a functioning channel of contact.

items.example: With all due respect, I believe your estimate overlooks two major costs.
items.note: A formal softener before disagreement; it may still sound confrontational or ironic.

items.example: You have missed the point: the question is about safety, not speed.
items.note: Miss the point means fail to grasp the main idea, not merely forget a detail.

items.example: The candidate faced a grilling about her previous management decisions.
items.note: A grilling is prolonged, tough questioning, often in interviews or public scrutiny.

items.pt: entender e reconhecer o seu argumento
items.example: I take your point about the budget, but I still favour the larger venue.
items.note: Take your point acknowledges that an argument is worth considering without full agreement.

items.example: The company issued a denial after reports of a planned factory closure.
items.note: Issue a denial is a formal public statement that an allegation is untrue.

items.example: The organiser gave a full apology for the confusion caused by the cancellation.
items.note: Give a full apology means apologise thoroughly and explicitly, often in a public setting.

items.example: The charity entered into a contract with a local catering company.
items.note: Enter into a contract is a formal phrase meaning become legally bound by an agreement.

items.example: The builder breached the contract by failing to complete the agreed repairs.
items.note: Breach means violate contractual obligations, not merely postpone the work.

items.example: The university made a firm commitment to fund the new programme for three years.
items.note: Firm strengthens commitment by stressing a definite intention rather than a tentative plan.

items.example: The customer sought compensation for a breach of contract.
items.note: This formal noun phrase refers to failure to fulfil contractual obligations.

items.example: With regard to the new timetable, we will publish an update on Friday.
items.note: A relatively formal linking phrase meaning concerning; followed by a noun phrase.
